definitions.label: O
definitions.name: O-Type Star
definitions.tooltip: O type stars are the hottest members of the familiar OBAFGKM spectral sequence, shining blue and producing intense ultraviolet radiation. Their enormous luminosity comes at a cost: massive O stars consume their nuclear fuel quickly and usually live for only a few million years. Their radiation and winds can carve cavities in nearby gas, light up nebulae, and influence the birth of other stars.
definitions.short_tooltip: An exceptionally hot, massive blue star.

definitions.label: B
definitions.name: B-Type Star
definitions.tooltip: B type stars are hot, blue white stars whose spectra place them just below O stars in temperature. Many are several times the Sun's mass and shine so intensely that they remain conspicuous across hundreds of light years. They burn their fuel faster than cooler stars and are common in young clusters, although a B spectrum alone does not prove that a star is young or on the main sequence.
definitions.short_tooltip: A hot, luminous blue-white star.

definitions.label: A
definitions.name: A-Type Star
definitions.tooltip: A type stars appear white or blue white and are best known for the strong hydrogen absorption lines in their spectra. They are hotter and usually more massive than the Sun, so a typical A star has a shorter main sequence lifetime and a brighter ultraviolet environment. Sirius A and Vega are nearby examples, but the class also includes stars at different evolutionary stages and some chemically or magnetically peculiar objects.
definitions.short_tooltip: A hot white or blue-white star.

definitions.label: F
definitions.name: F-Type Star
definitions.tooltip: F type stars are yellow white stars that bridge the gap between hot A stars and Sun like G stars. A typical main sequence F star is somewhat hotter and more massive than the Sun, radiates a larger share of ultraviolet light, and uses its fuel more quickly. Their planetary systems are interesting laboratories for studying how stellar lifetime and radiation shape planetary environments.
definitions.short_tooltip: A yellow-white star hotter than the Sun.

definitions.label: G
definitions.name: G-Type Star
definitions.tooltip: G type stars are yellow white stars in the same broad spectral class as the Sun. On the main sequence they can fuse hydrogen steadily for billions of years, while their spectra reveal the temperatures and atoms present in their atmospheres. The class also includes evolved subgiants and giants, so a G spectrum does not guarantee a star that resembles the Sun in age, size, planets, or habitability.
definitions.short_tooltip: A Sun-like yellow-white spectral class.

definitions.label: K
definitions.name: K-Type Star
definitions.tooltip: K type stars have orange light and cooler atmospheres than the Sun. Main sequence K dwarfs consume hydrogen slowly and can remain stable longer than G dwarfs, making their planetary systems especially interesting to astrobiologists. The same K spectrum can also belong to an evolved giant, so spectral temperature does not by itself reveal a star's size or age.
definitions.short_tooltip: A cooler orange stellar class.

definitions.label: M
definitions.name: M-Type Star
definitions.tooltip: M is the coolest major class in the traditional stellar sequence, producing red light and spectra rich in molecules. Most stars in the Galaxy are small M dwarfs that burn fuel extremely slowly, although young M dwarfs can also flare powerfully. Large evolved red giants may have the same M type atmosphere even though their size and history are entirely different.
definitions.short_tooltip: A cool red stellar class.

definitions.label: L
definitions.name: L-Type Ultracool Object
definitions.tooltip: L type objects are so cool that their spectra are shaped by metal hydrides, alkali lines, and clouds of mineral condensates. Most are brown dwarfs that never achieved sustained hydrogen fusion, but the warmest L objects can be stars with extremely low mass. Their faint visible glow gives way to much stronger infrared emission, where their complex weather and the boundary between stars and brown dwarfs can be studied.
definitions.short_tooltip: An ultracool L-type object.

definitions.label: T
definitions.name: T-Type Brown Dwarf
definitions.tooltip: T type brown dwarfs are cooler than L dwarfs, with infrared spectra strongly shaped by methane and water absorption. They do not sustain ordinary hydrogen fusion, so they gradually radiate away the heat left from their formation. Their masses overlap those of giant planets, making their spectra and formation history important to understanding what kind of object they are.
definitions.short_tooltip: A cool methane-bearing brown dwarf class.

definitions.label: Y
definitions.name: Y-Type Brown Dwarf
definitions.tooltip: Y type brown dwarfs occupy the coldest recognized brown dwarf spectral class, with some known examples having temperatures comparable to those found on Earth. At such low temperatures their atmospheres may contain ammonia and water bearing clouds, making them resemble giant planets more than conventional stars. They are extraordinarily faint in visible light and are found mainly through sensitive infrared surveys and searches for nearby moving objects.
definitions.short_tooltip: The coldest recognized brown-dwarf class.

definitions.label: WR
definitions.name: Wolf-Rayet Star
definitions.tooltip: Wolf-Rayet stars are hot, evolved stars whose spectra are dominated by broad emission lines from powerful, fast moving winds. Those winds have stripped away much of the outer star and exposed material altered by nuclear reactions, returning enriched gas to surrounding space. Many Wolf-Rayet stars began with very high masses, while some reached this state through mass transfer in binary systems.
definitions.short_tooltip: A hot evolved star with powerful winds.

definitions.label: WD
definitions.name: White Dwarf
definitions.tooltip: A white dwarf is the compact remnant left when a star with low or intermediate mass sheds its outer layers. Roughly a star's worth of mass can be compressed into a body about the size of Earth, supported by electron degeneracy pressure from quantum mechanics. With no sustained core fusion, it shines by releasing stored heat and cools over immense spans of time.
definitions.short_tooltip: A dense compact stellar remnant.

definitions.label: NS
definitions.name: Neutron Star
definitions.tooltip: A neutron star is the collapsed core left by some massive stars after core collapse. More than a Sun's worth of matter can be compressed into a sphere only tens of kilometers across, producing extraordinary density and surface gravity. Some neutron stars appear as pulsars or magnetars, while others are difficult to detect at all.
definitions.short_tooltip: An exceptionally dense stellar remnant.

definitions.label: PULSAR
definitions.name: Pulsar
definitions.tooltip: A pulsar is a rotating neutron star detected through remarkably regular pulses of radiation. Its magnetic field channels emission into beams that sweep through space; when a beam crosses Earth, telescopes record a pulse like the flash of a lighthouse. Pulse timing can reveal rotation, orbital motion, surrounding plasma, and even tiny disturbances in spacetime.
definitions.short_tooltip: A periodically observed rotating neutron star.

definitions.label: MAGNETAR
definitions.name: Magnetar
definitions.tooltip: A magnetar is a neutron star whose activity is powered largely by an exceptionally strong magnetic field. Stress in its crust and magnetic field can produce bursts of X rays and gamma rays, and rare giant flares can briefly become visible across a large part of the Galaxy. Magnetars rotate and slow down in ways that help astronomers estimate their magnetic behavior, although the internal field cannot be measured directly.
definitions.short_tooltip: A neutron star with an extreme magnetic field.

definitions.label: BH
definitions.name: Stellar-Mass Black Hole
definitions.tooltip: A stellar mass black hole forms when enough mass collapses inside an event horizon, a boundary from which light cannot return. The black hole itself emits no ordinary light, so astronomers infer it through effects such as a companion's orbit, gravitational waves, lensing, or radiation from nearby infalling matter. General relativity predicts a singularity inside, but present physics cannot tell us whether that mathematical prediction describes the true interior.
definitions.short_tooltip: An evidence supported stellar mass black hole.

definitions.label: 1 Known Star
definitions.name: One Known Stellar Member
definitions.tooltip: Only one star is currently known in this system. That may describe a genuinely solitary star, but faint, close, or face on companions can escape detection. New observations can therefore transform an apparently single star into a binary or multiple system.
definitions.short_tooltip: One accepted stellar member; unseen companions may exist.

definitions.label: Binary
definitions.name: Binary Star System
definitions.tooltip: A binary system contains two stars bound together by gravity. Both orbit their shared center of mass, or barycenter, with the more massive star moving on the smaller path. Binaries let astronomers measure stellar masses and test gravity because each star's motion constrains the other.
definitions.short_tooltip: Two accepted stellar members.

definitions.label: Multiple
definitions.name: Multiple Star System
definitions.tooltip: A multiple system contains at least three stars bound into one larger family. If several stars orbit at comparable distances, repeated gravitational encounters can exchange energy, alter orbits, or even eject a member. Long lived multiples therefore often organize themselves into separated orbital scales, such as a tight pair with a distant companion.
definitions.short_tooltip: Three or more accepted stellar members.

definitions.label: Hierarchical
definitions.name: Hierarchical Multiple System
definitions.tooltip: A system of three or more stars is difficult to preserve when every star tugs strongly on every other at comparable distances. Long lived multiples usually arrange themselves as nested orbits: a close pair acts almost like one combined mass to a much more distant companion, while still wider members can orbit the inner group. This separation of scales prevents many of the close encounters that would scramble or eject stars, allowing surprisingly complex stellar families to endure.
definitions.short_tooltip: Stellar members are organized into nested groups.

definitions.label: Planet Host
definitions.name: Confirmed Planet Host
definitions.tooltip: A confirmed planet host is a star system with at least one planet supported by published observations. Confirmation can come from transits, radial velocities, direct imaging, timing, microlensing, or other methods, each of which reveals different planetary properties. Candidates and false positives remain part of the discovery story, but they are not confirmed worlds.
definitions.short_tooltip: Hosts at least one confirmed planet.

definitions.label: USP
definitions.name: Ultra-Short-Period Planet
definitions.tooltip: An ultrashort period planet completes an entire orbit in less than one Earth day. Such a compact orbit places the planet close to its star, where intense irradiation, tidal forces, and atmospheric loss can reshape it. These systems test how planets migrate inward and how long they can survive near their stars.
definitions.short_tooltip: A confirmed planet orbiting in under one day.

definitions.label: HZ Screen
definitions.name: Habitable-Zone Screening Signal
definitions.tooltip: The habitable zone is the range of stellar energy where a rocky planet with a suitable atmosphere might sustain liquid water on its surface. Astronomers estimate this region from the star's energy output and climate models, but atmosphere, clouds, pressure, geology, and stellar activity can change the outcome. A planet in this zone is worth investigating; its location alone does not show that the world is habitable.
definitions.short_tooltip: A broad habitable zone screen, not a habitability claim.

definitions.label: Nearby
definitions.name: Nearby System
definitions.tooltip: This system lies within 25 light years of Sol. A light year is the distance light crosses in one year, so light from even the outer edge of this group reaches us within a human generation. These are the stars of our immediate astronomical neighborhood and some of the most practical targets for detailed study.
definitions.short_tooltip: Within 25 light years of Sol.

definitions.label: Local Neighborhood
definitions.name: Local Stellar Neighborhood
definitions.tooltip: This system lies between 25 and 100 light years from Sol. That volume contains a far broader sample of stars and planetary systems than our immediate neighborhood while remaining close on the scale of the Milky Way. Light reaching us from its outer edge began traveling about a century ago.
definitions.short_tooltip: Between 25 and 100 light years from Sol.

definitions.label: Hot Giant
definitions.name: Hot Giant Planet
definitions.tooltip: A hot giant is a large confirmed planet that receives intense energy from its star. Many orbit close enough for their atmospheres to expand, circulate at extreme speeds, or escape into space. Size and heating make these effects possible, but they do not reveal the planet's exact composition, clouds, or rings.
definitions.short_tooltip: A hot, giant scale confirmed planet.

definitions.label: Temperate Giant
definitions.name: Temperate Giant Planet
definitions.tooltip: A temperate giant is a large confirmed planet receiving a moderate level of energy from its star. A giant planet is not expected to offer an Earth like solid surface, but its atmosphere and any moons could make the system scientifically compelling. Its temperature category describes stellar heating rather than a known climate.
definitions.short_tooltip: A temperate, giant scale confirmed planet.

definitions.label: Cold Giant
definitions.name: Cold Giant Planet
definitions.tooltip: A cold giant is a large confirmed planet receiving relatively little energy from its star. Such worlds often occupy wide, long period orbits where volatile compounds can condense and the planet's internal heat may remain important. Their clouds, composition, moons, and rings are separate questions that require closer observation.
definitions.short_tooltip: A cold, giant scale confirmed planet.

definitions.label: Hot Neptunian
definitions.name: Hot Neptunian Planet
definitions.tooltip: A hot Neptunian lies in the broad size or mass range between terrestrial worlds and giants while receiving intense stellar energy. This group may include rocky cores with thick envelopes as well as volatile rich worlds losing gas under strong irradiation. Similar size does not guarantee a Neptune like composition or interior.
definitions.short_tooltip: A hot, Neptune scale confirmed planet.

definitions.label: Temperate Neptunian
definitions.name: Temperate Neptunian Planet
definitions.tooltip: A temperate Neptunian lies in the broad size or mass range between terrestrial worlds and giants while receiving moderate stellar energy. Planets in this range have no exact Solar System counterpart and may include deep atmospheres, volatile rich interiors, or large oceans beneath high pressure. These possibilities make them fascinating targets, but size and heating alone cannot reveal their surfaces or habitability.
definitions.short_tooltip: A temperate, Neptune scale screening class.

definitions.label: Cold Neptunian
definitions.name: Cold Neptunian Planet
definitions.tooltip: A cold Neptunian lies in the broad size or mass range between terrestrial worlds and giants while receiving relatively little stellar energy. It could resemble an ice giant, a gas rich super Earth, or something with no close Solar System analogue. Neptunian describes a useful scale, not a measured composition.
definitions.short_tooltip: A cold, Neptune scale confirmed planet.

definitions.label: Hot Terrestrial
definitions.name: Hot Terrestrial Planet
definitions.tooltip: A hot terrestrial is a confirmed planet in the smallest broad size or mass range while receiving intense stellar energy. Some may have rocky surfaces, lava regions, or eroded atmospheres, while worlds near the category boundary may retain substantial volatile envelopes. Size and heating make those scenarios testable but do not choose between them.
definitions.short_tooltip: A hot, terrestrial scale confirmed planet.

definitions.label: Temperate Terrestrial
definitions.name: Temperate Terrestrial Planet
definitions.tooltip: A temperate terrestrial is a confirmed planet in the smallest broad size or mass range while receiving moderate stellar energy. That combination makes it an obvious target in the search for rocky, potentially clement worlds, but it does not reveal an atmosphere, ocean, magnetic field, or biosphere. Even a planet in the habitable zone can resemble Venus, Mars, or something unfamiliar.
definitions.short_tooltip: A temperate terrestrial scale screening class.

definitions.label: Cold Terrestrial
definitions.name: Cold Terrestrial Planet
definitions.tooltip: A cold terrestrial is a confirmed planet in the smallest broad size or mass range while receiving relatively little energy from its star. Its surface could be rocky, ice covered, volatile rich, or hidden beneath an atmosphere, and internal or tidal heating may matter as much as starlight. Weak irradiation does not make a world geologically inactive or scientifically dull.
definitions.short_tooltip: A cold, terrestrial scale confirmed planet.
